utterances.text: And my question is: Without official confirmation, such as a DNA identification report, we can't really tell who the remains of that body belonged to, can we?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the body that you referred to, that body could have been placed at that location at any time prior to its discovery; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally participated in the exhumation of that body. The way of identification -- in addition to the DNA method, there is also the so-called classical identification. That is when family members can visually identify their next of kin without having to resort to the DNA method. In that case, the DNA method is only an auxiliary method.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And we've heard no evidence of a classical identification, have we?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's because all the bodies that we're discussing here were identified by the DNA method, so there was no need to mention the classical method. But what I'm saying is that in addition to the DNA method, there is also the classical way of identifying a body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn to a different location where body remains were discovered. Is it your understanding that the remains of a person named "Gojko Vujicic" was found in Bosici village, together with two other bodies belonging to Predrag Kanesovic and Bogoljub Topic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bodies were discovered in Bosici, a place called Bosici, not Vozuca. It is in Zavidovici Municipality, but the place is actually a meadow called "Bosici," and I personally participated in the exhumation of those bodies. I was the one who discovered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And can you confirm for us that the location of Bosici village is approximately about 27 kilometres away from the 13th kilometre by the Gostovici River?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be anything between 25 and 30. One would actually have to look at the map and measure the distance, but I would say that you were approximately right, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then the final body remains that I want to discuss with you. At paragraph 40 of your statement, you say that remains were found at Djurica Vis, and it's your understanding that those remains belonged to Zivinko Todorovic. Is that what you say in your statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of the location is Bare, you're right. I personally found the body, I participated in the exhumation, and I worked on that body up until the moment when it was identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that, during the proceedings today and yesterday, no forensic evidence has been put before the Trial Chamber confirming the identification of those body remains as being Zivinko Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, in fairness to this witness, does this witness know the witnesses who have testified before this Tribunal before him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said "during the proceedings today and yesterday," so I'm referring specifically to this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Certainly, and he has been saying he's not the doctor. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Are you able to answer that question or please say so if you can't.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: During the course of your testimony today and yesterday, have you seen any evidence confirming that the remains of the body found at Djurica Vis belonged to Zivinko Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I submitted evidence to the Prosecution, but it hasn't been presented here, the evidence concerning Zivinko Todorovic from the Bare locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, moving away from discovery of bodies and so on, I'd like to turn to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for the translation, and I would also like to know: According to what you know, Zivinko Todorovic was identified, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat that? I'm not sure that I understood you properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To your knowledge, Zivinko Todorovic, was he identified?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was identified, and his body was handed over to the family for burial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to which method, a classical method or the DNA method, was he identified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 2002 or 2003, he was identified by the DNA method. I'm actually not sure about the years, so I don't want to make any mistakes there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I could turn to the photograph that were shown by the Prosecution yesterday. If the document could please be brought up on the screen, I believe it's Exhibit 648.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krcmar, we can see a picture with five men in this room, and you say the men have been identified. Would you agree with me that the quality of this photograph is quite poor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's clarify one thing. These men were not identified. They were recognised by the families in the photo, but their bodies were never found. They were never buried. They were only recognised by the families in the photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I think there might have been some -- we might have been at cross-purposes. That's what I was driving at, Mr. Krcmar. You say that these five men were recognised, but you'd agree with me that the quality of the photograph is quite poor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photo we see, it looks poor, but other methods were used. The photos were blown up. Parts of the photos were blown up in order to enable the families to recognise their faces. But if you look at the photo even as it is now, I'm sure that every family would be able to recognise their next of kin in that photo. If I were a family member, I'm sure I would recognise these men if they were my next of kin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'm not disputing that, Mr. Krcmar. I'd be grateful if you could please focus on the question you've been asked. As you look at this photograph, it's of poor quality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It really depends on the person. It would be ever so important to me if I had more of such photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can see that the room is bare, can't we? There are no distinguishing features, such as any picture, or wallpaper, or anything like that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You can't tell how many windows are in the room or the size of the room, can you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in this room. I can even specify the dimensions, although I had no measuring tape on hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Again, I'll repeat what I said before, if you could please focus on my question. From looking at this photograph, you can't tell how many windows are in the room or its size, can you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the photograph alone, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And as we look at the wall behind the five men, we can see markings; and, certainly to me, it's unclear whether those markings might be caused by water or perhaps it may be due to plaster coming away from the walls. We can't tell, can we?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what caused this, whether it was something hard or caused by water, but we see the damage on the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can't -- from looking at this photograph, we can't tell if it's a room within a house, or a room in a garage, or a room within any other type of building, can we?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in a building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: But you would agree with me, we can't tell what type of building it is from this photograph?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that. In my statement -- or rather, in my testimony yesterday, I said I was in this room. I identified that room precisely, based on the damage on the walls that can be seen here. I even know who owns the property.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Focus on the photograph and the questions I'm asking you: This room could look like thousands of rooms in buildings in that part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the sake of argument, let's say "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you'd agree with me that many buildings during the war would have similar types of markings as what we can see here, caused by damage from the war or perhaps if the building had been neglected?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This property - and I'm telling you the truth - is what I visited in 1997, in late November. This photograph, I am 100 per cent certain, tallies or corresponds to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Please, sir --

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm listening. I'm all ears.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We'll come to your visit there in a moment, but the question I've asked you is: You'd agree that many buildings in that area would have similar markings like the ones we can see in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Similar perhaps, yes; not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you said that the photograph was taken on the 17th of September, 1995. I'm right in saying that the reason you've given that date is because we can see some figures in the bottom right-hand corner of this photograph? You say that is the date generated by the camera?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what one can read there. All of us can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that you have no way of knowing whether that date feature was set correctly on the camera or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not stating either way. I'm just going by what I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, in your evidence, you claimed that you knew the location where this photograph was taken because, in November 1997, you went into the room and carried out a reconstruction of the photograph, and you said there was identical damage on the wall. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, you've been interviewed twice by the Office of the Prosecution, in connection with the disappearance of missing VRS soldiers, in December of 2005 and June of 2007. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in neither of those statements do you mention that you have direct knowledge that soldiers were kept in the Mujahedin camp. We know, from what you've told us today, that you told the investigator about what you were told by two VRS soldiers back in 1998, but I'm interested as to why you didn't mention that you claimed that you went to the Mujahedin camp yourself. Wouldn't this have been something worth mentioning to the investigator, Mr. Krcmar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned from several sources about missing persons and their whereabouts, inter alia Gostovici. My statement would have been far more voluminous had I mentioned all of this. I have been going back and forth for years now. I only mention in my statement what I thought was of key importance. As far as I recall, this photograph was handed over to the Prosecution by myself. I think you have had it before that, though; but now we have it before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You didn't think it was of key importance to mention to the investigator something that you claimed to have direct knowledge of. Let me move on. You've mentioned this photograph and your visit to -- that you claim to have made to the camp for the very first time on the 22nd of October of this year, when you met with Ms. Sartorio; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was much earlier that I talked to the investigators about my going to the camp, and I even think that I was there with one of the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, we have a proofing note of what you discussed -- well, first of all, let's confirm. You did meet with Ms. Sartorio three days ago on the 22nd of October. I think you verified that already.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And that was in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, as I say, we have the proofing note and I can show it if necessary, but you told Ms. Sartorio that you visited the camp in 1998 and saw markings on the wall. There was no mention made of you going there and conducting a reconstruction of the photo.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there in 1997, in late November or in the second half of November. And as for the Prosecutor, I mentioned and described the damage on the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If you were adamant you were there in 1997, why is it that only three days ago you told Ms. Sartorio that your visit was in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I object. Well, this is a proofing note that I wrote, so I don't believe he can ask the witness if he ever he looked at my proofing notes, because this is me, my notes to the Defence counsel. So he can ask the witness whether that's what he recollects telling me or ask the witness if he read my proofing notes. I just -- this witness cannot be held accountable for what my proofing notes are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can certainly do that. We would expect proofing notes to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krcmar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But do you hold this witness for the accuracy of the proofing note, or do you hold Ms. Sartorio for the accuracy?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'll do is I'll take on board my learned friend's comments, and I'll ask the correct question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krcmar, did you tell Ms. Sartorio that you'd visited the camp in 1998 when you met with her three days ago?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I showed her this photograph, which you already had knowledge of, as far as I could judge from her reaction. But I can repeat, I was there in late 1997, in November. If there is a discrepancy in terms of dates, I'm poor when it comes to remembering dates. For 12 years, I've been going out in the field. It is difficult for me to recall an exact date without a document being put in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So now that you accept that you told the Prosecutor a different date from the date that you now say you were there, let me ask you something else: Why didn't you tell Ms. Sartorio that you had carried out a reconstruction of this photograph, as you explained to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I object again to the form. He can ask me if he told me that. Again, he's making this witness repeat -- well, he's trying to say that that is exactly what he said, and proofing notes are what my -- what I take down. I don't take down every word. We don't have a stenographer at the proofing sessions. So, again, it shouldn't be used in court against this or with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that when you met Ms. Sartorio three days ago, you made no mention of carrying out a previous reconstruction of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree, I disagree. We carried out that reconstruction, we discussed the photograph, and we discussed the damage on the wall. I don't know what was entered into evidence, but I don't know what we discussed [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And this reconstruction of the photograph you said that you carried out, you haven't brought any documents along showing the reconstruction or anything like that, have you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was there on the spot, and I testify here under oath. I'm saying I was there in November 1997, say, the 25th of November or later. I was there. I carried out a reconstruction. I don't know what documents you wanted me to have here if I'm telling you I was there. I'm telling you that these people were recognised by their family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If you'd attended the camp and gone into a room and recognised it, as you say you did, either in 1997 or in 1998, you should have made some sort of record of that, shouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have such records. It should be contained in the reports that I sent to my office. I report on my field trips upon my return to the office; however, at that moment we were still looking for 460 people. It is difficult to record every detail you see in the field. Perhaps, at that time, it doesn't amount to much, but later it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The reality is, Mr. Krcmar, that this room could be one of thousands of rooms that existed in that part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be, but it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the fact is that you can't recognise the room, and you have no way of knowing which room these men were in. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. You're trying to persuade me that I wasn't there. I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Before we leave this photograph, as I recollect from your testimony yesterday, you said that two of the men - indeed, it's written on here - two of the men, we have Dragan Lukic and Marko Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I could go back to the ABiH handwritten list, please, for a moment, it's Exhibit 646. It's the ABiH handwritten list. That's the one that I'm after. As everybody has a copy of that, I don't think there's any need for us to wait for it to appear on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krcmar, if you could please look through this list, would you agree with me that neither Dragan Lukic nor Marko Maric appear upon this list?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this list, these two persons' names do not appear. However, on the list I compiled, they appear under items 5 and 46. It reads there "Marucic," but it wasn't Marucic, but Maric, Marko and Lukic, Dragan. Under 5, you have Dragutin Lukic. I keep referring to the revised list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. So they weren't there. Now, the final point --

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: My final issue, Mr. Krcmar: Judge Harhoff asked you a question about paragraph 19 of your statement, and that is the part where you state: "We have confirmed that six of the seven persons were VRS soldiers captured by the ABiH and handed over to the Mujahedin at Kesten." Could you tell us, who were the sources of this information? Who informed you about this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The six identified persons from the list, and the seventh one being Mladen Pejic, were found in the same grave in Kamenica. The sources are DNA reports and identification on the part of family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The question you were asked by Judge Harhoff related to the capture of certain persons by the ABiH, who then handed them over to the Mujahedin at Kesten. Now, you weren't present that day, were you? You have no personal knowledge of what happened. You would agree with me?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Had I been there, I wouldn't have -- I wouldn't be sitting here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, please, could you tell us, if you're able to, who was it that told you that VRS soldiers had been captured by the ABiH and handed over to the Mujahedin at Kesten?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information came from several sources. The first one was the exchange of prisoners from the Zenica Prison in 1995, on the 24th of December. The second one was on the 27th of January, 1996. The people who left the prison told me that in Gostovici there were 64 POWs. Another source were the three surviving women. Allow me to finish. Another piece of information is since Bosnia-Herzegovina is a small country, people know each other. The missing people's families were in contact. They were looking for their loved ones, and they learned that there were 64 men held at the camp. The third source was the Commission. During negotiations with the commission for Bosnia-Herzegovina, they told me there was a camp of a sizeable group. They didn't mention a figure, but they also told me that at that moment they were unable to discuss that. There were several different sources of information. And even later, in 1997 and 1998, the local population, the Bosniaks living there, told us of a large group of people who were taken from Kesten to Gostovici, to the camp. There were several different unrelated sources. And to conclude, the list that appeared confirmed that we had found six of those people at Kamenica and identified them. What else do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just to go back to the -- one of the last sources of information you've mentioned, you said, "in 1997 and 1998, the local population, the Bosniaks living there." It's right, isn't it, that during the war, and particularly in 1995, there were no Bosniaks living in Kesten and that area?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the people from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were there in other units as part of the 2nd and 3rd Corps of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that there were no members of the local population who were living in that area at the time who could have passed on information to you about what happened during 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not civilians. There were military formations there comprising the people of Ozren, from the village of Delici and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So just to conclude, what you have stated in paragraph 19 of your statement is simply recalling or repeating what others have told you and no more?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I wasn't there in 1995, but I've been doing research and investigating the case for 12 years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Krcmar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robson. Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I have maybe ten minutes, Your Honour, but I don't know if you want to take a break. It's up to you, but I would like to also, for the record, I withdraw the objection in terms of authenticity of that prior document. I don't think that -- I think our office received it, and I apologise for that. I recognise that it probably came from the Ministry of Defence, so I don't want that on the record that I object to the authenticity. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well, Madam Sartorio --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well, Madam Sartorio, but I think it doesn't change the issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, are you done?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I've finished, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Robson. Madam Sartorio, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Just a short ten or 15 minutes, Your Honour. Thank you. May the witness be shown Exhibit P06176, P06176.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is the front of the document, but can you identify this document at this point?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is photo documentation for Zivinko Todorovic, son of Savo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And could we go to the last -- well, actually it's page 7 of the document, at least the English. Could you enlarge the English, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we having any technical problems?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It's page 14 of the Bosnian version and 7 of the English. I don't have the English. Do the Judges have the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't have. The usher's computer is having problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. There it is. Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the file card of a missing or detained person, a document issued by the Office for Missing Persons. This particular one belongs to Zivinko Todorovic and contains all the data that my office has. We saw a number of such file cards yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. And was this -- this is the person that you referred to in your statement and which you were asked about by Defence counsel on cross-examination; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Could we go two more pages into this document, please. Right there for the English. You don't have to go any further, and the next page for the Bosnian, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Chamber what this document is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report of the identification of mortal remains for Zivinko Todorovic, and we can see the signatures of the members of the family and persons competent for the identification. All their signatures are there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And I believe that you testified, or if you didn't, were you present at the exhumation of this body?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found the location, and I also attended the exhumation of this body.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would ask that this document be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 652.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, can we go back to the handwritten list one more time, please. It's 646, the exhibit number, and the beginning. I'll wait for the English. Actually, there's no English. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, number 5, I know you've talked about this quite a bit, but, looking at number 5, did you ever find anyone in your database with the first name "Dragutin Lukic" with that date of birth and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't have anybody called "Dragutin Lukic." We only have a "Dragan Lukic."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And if you scroll down to number 10 -- well, you don't need to scroll.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, did you ever find anyone -- has anyone ever been reported missing to your office or have you ever -- during your research, or anyone in your computer by the name of Bozidar Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We don't have anybody by the name of Bozidar Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But do you have someone by the name of Bozidar Torovic [sic]. Right? That was one of the --

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: All right. If you scroll down to number 9, does your computer -- do your records show that there was a Radovan Radojcic, as spelled there? Is that a correct spelling of that name?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't have a Radovan Radojcic. We have Radenko Radojcic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And number 16, in your computer and your database, do you have someone missing, unaccounted for, and it was Cedo Dabic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we had that person. That person was identified and buried. I don't know whether this is a spelling mistake. This list has to be collated with my list. But, in any case, that person was identified on the 29th of November, 2006, and buried.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And number 33.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If we may scroll down to 33.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stjepanovic, and it says "Drago" here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And is that name correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Stjepanovic" is correct. I don't know whether the name is Draguslob or something else. I don't remember and I don't want to speculate. Again, I am referring you to my table. I've had 5.000 names to deal with. I don't know what the correct name is; but in any case, I know who this is, I know that the body was found and buried.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And, number 66, did you have anyone in your system by the name of Mirko Maricic? Was there anyone that you found that was reported missing or you found was missing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio, number 66?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Forty-six, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Forty-six, you're correct. Sorry. It looks like -- sorry, 46. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here "Marko Maricic." His name is Maric, Marko, and the father's name is Marko as well. He was born in Podsjelovo in Zavidovici Municipality, born in 1946. He was not located ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, previously this witness has expressed an unwillingness to comment on documents not prepared by him. It's been put to him by the Prosecutor that this name, Mirko Maricic, is somebody else. The question -- the objection I pose is: Is he in a position to say the correct name has not been put down on this list? He's told us he's not the author, so I'm just wondering whether he can answer the question that's been put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm trying to look for the question you say was put to the witness by Madam Sartorio. You say Madam Sartorio put to him that this name, Mirko Maricic, is somebody else. Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, at line 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Line 14 is the witness speaking or am I talking?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No. In the question, I say: "In number 66, did you have anyone in your system by the name of Mirko Maricic?" I'm not asking him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that's the same as saying is this somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No. I am not asking him that. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to check with Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps Madam Sartorio can continue, and we'll see where it goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: My question is, sir, in your database and in your research for the RS Commission for Missing Persons in the last 12 years, have you ever located or been told of a person who is missing by the name of Mirko Maricic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. M.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Sartorio. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Honourable Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge, the interpreters asked for your microphone, please, madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one question. I am not even quite sure whether I should ask you. Yes, let me ask you. You've been asking, sir, that you be shown the list that you have compiled, that you collated. This one. I haven't seen it being shown to you. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not here. I have submitted it to the Prosecutor's Office with all files, for every person, and even the addresses of the families of the persons on the handwritten list. All the corrections have been made, and for every person a file was submitted similar to the one that we've just seen on the screen. I just wanted to make sure that you understand that the lists are more or less the same. They're more or less identical, save for the typos that existed in the original list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand, sir. Now, you say you gave it to the Prosecution. Have you been shown that list in the last two days that you have been testifying here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You mean my list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I understood you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have been shown your list in the last two days?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm just sympathising because even begging for this list and it's not coming, and I don't understand why it's not coming. Anyway. Thank you so much. You don't have to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This brings us to the conclusion of -- I beg your pardon. Any questions arising from the questions by me, Madam Sartorio?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. That brings us to the end of your testimony. We thank you very much for taking time off from your very busy schedule to come and testify, and we hope you have a safe journey back home. You are now excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio, the Chamber has received a note here from VWS, I suppose that is this, concerning the next witness. I'll just read it out, and maybe you have better instructions and you can tell us. It says: "The witness that's due to testify shortly. She is terribly upset. Through no fault of her own, her luggage was lost on the flight yesterday. Crucial papers relating to her testimony, largely statistics explaining her case, were lost with her suitcase. The suitcase is now recovered, however. She received the suitcase from one of our drivers only one hour ago; therefore, we are asking for her testimony to be delayed so that she is able to prepare herself properly before her appearance in court. Please advise Chambers of the matter. I believe the testimony she would give if asked to proceed immediately would not be on an acceptable standard, considering that she is very upset and has not been able to prepare properly." Have you heard anything about this witness, ma'am, in addition to what I've just read?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I spoke with her personally, and that's what she told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Given that, the Chamber filed a decision sometime either early this week or last week in response to the Defence motion asking for a four-day sitting session; and according to the schedule, we were therefore supposed to be off on Monday. This witness is here already. We would like to propose that we sit on Monday and maybe take Friday off, just to accommodate this witness, because she's here already, unless she's going back now. If she's going back, then we can start on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No. She's not going back, Your Honour, but I did ask her about her availability, and she is available on Monday, even on Tuesday. She doesn't have to be back. That proposal may not be a bad idea, because I think we may have to postpone or move a witness or two from the end of next week if we don't sit on Monday. We were anticipating that we would be sitting on Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. The order said we would not be sitting on Mondays, where possible. That's a scheduling problem, and this coming here, the scheduling office was able to accommodate us on Monday. So, according to the schedule, we are not supposed to be sitting on Monday, and this suggestion that we sit on Monday is based simply on the fact that there is a desire to accommodate this witness and the Tribunal, so that we don't sit here Monday doing nothing and we are paying for a witness in a hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's fine with the Prosecution, Your Honour. That's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that acceptable to everybody?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have no microphone, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say that I am not very happy, because we are really overworked; but given the situation, obviously we will accept that proposal, bearing in mind that the witness is important and she is here, and we have to accommodate her, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your consideration, Madam Vidovic. Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We would propose perhaps, though, that we do sit through the whole week next week, because the following week, it's going to put all the other days off. I believe the following week, we're off on Tuesday -- Monday or Tuesday, so it would be a Friday and a Monday, I think. In other words, I don't know what the day off next week is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know what the day off the week after next is, but let's see if we can find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Sartorio, I thought you just said that it would be convenient for the Prosecution to put off some witnesses for next week's schedule.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, I did, but my colleague discussed it with me and said it might require some juggling with witnesses, and I'm not sure what their availability is going to be until we can talk to them. We anticipated contacting them anyway because we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you say what you want to say, we are just being advised that according to the schedule, we are not sitting on the 6th of November, which is the week after, and that the 6th of November is a Tuesday. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really have to say that we need that day, because we are expecting some very difficult witnesses, bearing in mind that we only received transcript at the last moment, which the Prosecution knows very well. And, second of all, for medical reasons and for reasons of the well-being of my team, I would kindly ask you to stick to the schedule as you decided, to only work four days a week, and to have either a Monday or a Friday off. The day doesn't really make a difference, but we need that one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll agree to that and just deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. In that event, then, we are sitting on Monday next week, the 29th of October, at quarter past 2.00, Courtroom II. Court adjourned -- I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a housekeeping matter, if I may. I apologise for not getting up to my feet any faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it relates to Rule 92 ter witnesses. The Trial Chamber may be aware the Prosecution have written to the Defence and indicated they may want to call approximately ten witnesses or so using this procedure. Obviously, we've just had the first 92 ter witness, so to a certain extent I think we are testing the waters a little. What I would like to put on the record is that the way it went with the last witness didn't really accord with the Defence's view or idea as to how it should have gone. The Defence was of the view that with this type of witness, the Prosecution would call the witness, ask a few questions to establish the voracity of any statement, then perhaps just deal with any small matters of clarification, and then hand over to the Defence. Obviously, with the last witness we had the statements, plus we had two hours or so of effectively viva voce --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: -- evidence. Three. The Defence are trying to propose this in a collegial manner and trying to agree, to the largest extent possible, with the Prosecution that witnesses can be used in accordance with this Rule, but we feel that with the last witness, it wasn't in keeping with the spirit of Rule 92 ter. So, although this witness did deal with some complex matters, the Defence would indicate that there are more important witnesses to come which the Prosecution have indicated will be called pursuant to Rule 92 ter, and we would just like to note for the record that we wouldn't like to see a similar situation whereby witness statements are introduced that the Defence have to prepare in relation to for cross-examination, and then in addition we have a significant amount of viva voce evidence that we then also have to deal with. If all the other witnesses are going to follow in a similar manner, it may mean that we may have to take a bit more of a robust approach and perhaps not -- and indicate our displeasure to the Trial Chamber, if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, thank you very much for raising that point. It was the intention of the Chamber to raise it, but it slipped my mind. You've heard what Mr. Robson has said, Ms. Sartorio, and before you respond I just want to say to you that, as the Chamber, we were thinking very seriously of dropping the idea of using 92 ter witnesses if this is the way things are going to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I will take full responsibility for that. As I said yesterday, we talked and perhaps this wasn't an appropriate 92 ter witness. And, also, one of the issues is that normally the Trial Chamber, I believe, is -- a motion is filed and the Trial Chamber's given the statements in advance; therefore, you're able to read the statements so that the follow-up questions are put in context. I realise yesterday that that wasn't the case. So the way I understood some questions from the Bench early on, I felt there was going to be confusion if I didn't go back over the testimony and try to lay some foundation or context. So I would propose that we -- if we are going to do it, that the Defence counsel agree to us submitting the statements in advance so that Your Honours can read the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But this is what has been happening. Is there any rule that says because a witness is 92 ter, you don't have to submit a statement in advance?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Is there any rule that says we don't or do? --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not that I'm aware of, because it didn't happen in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then why didn't it happen in this case?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't -- I don't know why. I guess I didn't think it could happen, but I guess I was wrong. It could have been done, and I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You didn't think it could happen?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I didn't think that we were allowed to do that, even though there's no rule. I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yet you are allowed to do that with a viva voce witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Allowed to do what with a viva voce?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To give an advance statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We don't give advance statements to the Court with viva voce witnesses. His statements aren't in evidence, is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I receive statements every day before, in fact --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If I could perhaps seek some clarification. The proper way, at least in my view, to apply Rule 92 ter is, of course, to rely on the statement which we have. The issue is, then, if further documents can be admitted through the witness. That is basically the issue. If you have a huge number of documents in mind, then my advice would be that you should then go for 92 bis. However, if you do choose to go down the avenue of 92 ter in order to save time, then I think that two things need to be adhered to. One is that if you wish to have documents admitted through a 92 ter witness, then in any case that has to be a very small number, one or two documents and that's about it. Secondly, those documents should be documents that relate to simple points of clarification of what is in the statement and should not be documents that import a whole series of other documents and import issues which will need extensive examination-in-chief. So if you can steer clear of those two caveats, then I think 92 ter is a good way to go ahead, but you have to be careful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to add, to avoid Judges asking questions which will be mooted in preliminary statements, it would be better to have them before, and this would solve one of the problems. But the question asked by Defence is much wider and concerns those problems which also Judge Harhoff has expressed; therefore, presenting preliminary statements to the Chamber does not actually solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. The problem is with the fact that this was the first 92 ter, and it was a testing for myself. Again, I take personal responsibility for going over, and I think we will take what Judge Harhoff has said and what you have said very, very seriously in the future in terms of 92 ter witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I think, as a rule, any witness who's been led pursuant to 92 ter should not be asked viva voce questions for more than five to seven minutes. You're just introducing the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see you are --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this has actually been a subject of much discussion lately in the entire OTP, and there's been a lot of group e-mails going around. What I've learned from this is that in the other -- I think the other six trials, that they are allowed to do some viva voce outside the statement, up to 60 minutes is what a lot of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Up to 60 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. It generally averages between 30 and 60 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In my view, if you're going to take 60 minutes, you might as well lead the witness viva voce. Sorry. I don't see how much more time you are saving.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: If you've got to take 60 minutes to lead a 92 ter witness, how much would you have taken were you to deal with that witness viva voce? What would have been your estimate of the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: With this particular one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no. A witness about whom you take 60 minutes to lead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, hopefully less than that, if it's done correctly. That is the purpose of why we're asking for 92 ter. This was not a good -- is not a good example that I set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no. You see, you're talking about this example. I'm not talking about this example.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Listen to what I have said. You say in other trials you are given something like 60 minutes, in other Chambers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm saying if you have a witness who's 92 ter, and you need 60 minutes to introduce that witness, how much would you have taken if you had led that same witness viva voce?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, I can't think of many witnesses we've done in less than 60 minutes in this trial viva voce; very few, I think. So I think it does save some time, but I would think that the 60 minutes is all relative. If it's a witness that was scheduled for three hours, then it might be 60 minutes. If the witness is only scheduled for an hour, then I would propose that we would be -- it wouldn't make any sense to direct the witness for 60 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Madam Sartorio, the whole purpose of 92 ter is to save on time --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- so that there's not much time wasted by the leading team, and then the time is used for cross-examination. I don't think that 60 minutes is saving time on a 92 ter, but my colleagues might have something to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have nothing to add to this, Mr. President. I just wanted to clarify a small mistake that I made in my intervention in saying that the alternative to 92 ter was 92 bis, which of course was a mistake. I meant to say "65 ter," of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just a final point, Your Honour. Just in response to what Ms. Sartorio is saying, that the Prosecution be permitted to have up to 60 minutes to examine a Rule 65 witness viva voce -- I beg your pardon, 92 ter. I would just like to point out that could well have an impact on the length of time the Defence needs to cross-examine, because obviously we need time to deal with the statement, and we would need an additional period of time to deal with the 60 minutes. It raises the question of are we really saving --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. If you're going to take an hour, you might as well lead viva voce, because then you're really expanding. You may be saving time on the leading side, but you're expanding it on the cross-examining side, so it does not serve the purpose of 92 ter. So you might as well go viva voce.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would suggest that we take the next witness and do it within a short period of time, and make a decision after that if we're not able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. We're not making a decision now. We're just sounding a warning now that, look, if this happens again, then we're going to cancel all your 92 ter --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- witnesses, and then you'll have to lead them through viva voce.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Any other housekeeping matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From your side, Madam Sartorio?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From the Bench? Thank you. We'll take a break. I did say we would adjourn to Monday, the 29th, at quarter past 2.00, Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 29th day of October, 2007, at 2.00 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
